title: Correspondents Lunch

jokes.text: We saw the bus stop where a young Barack Obama used to sit and wait for the bus. - Theoretically. - It's possible.
jokes.setup: Leslie excitedly describes their honeymoon highlight as a mundane bus stop connected to Obama.
jokes.punchline: Ben and Leslie's immediate 'Theoretically / It's possible' undercuts the claim — they have no evidence Obama ever actually sat there.
jokes.explanation: A tight two-beat joke that perfectly captures Leslie's over-enthusiasm and Ben's grounding rationality. The rapid back-and-forth 'Theoretically / It's possible' is a great couple rhythm — they're both in on the delusion. Strong character integration and economy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This is the exact spot where Abraham Lincoln stayed the night before he gave the Gettysburg Address. Can you imagine? We're standing exactly where Lincoln stood.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Actually, I'm pretty sure he gave the address in Gettysburg, Pennsylvania, and this is Ohio.

jokes.text: Then we went and visited Honolulu City Hall... Well, it looked amazing, but it was closed.
jokes.setup: Leslie describes their honeymoon itinerary including visiting a city hall — which is already absurd as a romantic destination.
jokes.punchline: It was closed. The ultimate anticlimax of an already absurd tourism choice.
jokes.explanation: A pitch-perfect Leslie Knope joke. Only Leslie would visit city hall on her honeymoon and only Leslie would still be dazzled even though it was closed. The joke works on two levels: the absurdity of the choice AND the tragicomic disappointment. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, I can't believe we're finally here at the National Archives! This is the most romantic honeymoon destination ever!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, I love your enthusiasm, but we've been standing outside for twenty minutes. We can't actually go in.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? Why not?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: It's closed for renovation. For the next three months.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh.

jokes.text: Donna, we got you some coffee, because you said, 'I like my coffee like I like my men. Dark, rich, and full-bodied.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is distributing personalized gifts from Hawaii.
jokes.punchline: Donna's quote about coffee is a classic double entendre delivered as a straight fact, with Donna's 'Yes, indeed' confirming her brand.
jokes.explanation: The 'I like my X like I like my men' template is an old joke format, but Donna's character makes it land — her unapologetic sensuality is a cornerstone of her persona. 'Yes, indeed' is a perfect Donna button. Loses points for originality since the template is very familiar.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We found this amazing Hawaiian fertility tea at this little shop downtown, and it was so affordable, and the guy said if we bought in bulk he'd give us an even better deal, and he said he could deliver it right to our house, and—wait.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God. We bought drugs from a drug dealer.

jokes.text: Ann, we got you some very rare Hawaiian fertility tea... the busboy told us about a guy in a parking lot with a backpack full of this stuff, and I'm just realizing now that it's not tea. And I'm gonna throw it away.
jokes.setup: Leslie presents rare Hawaiian fertility tea as a thoughtful gift for Ann who wants a baby.
jokes.punchline: As Leslie narrates the sourcing — busboy, parking lot, guy with a backpack — she mid-sentence realizes she bought Ann drugs, pivots to 'I'm gonna throw it away.'
jokes.explanation: This is a standout joke with excellent structure. The slow-burn revelation is perfectly paced — each detail (busboy, parking lot, backpack full of stuff) adds a beat of dawning horror, and the pivot to 'I'm just realizing now that it's not tea. And I'm gonna throw it away' is executed with deadpan mastery. The abrupt pragmatic resolution is a great button. Strong character integration: only Leslie would tell this story with such earnest momentum before catching herself.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I got you this statue of an angry god because it reminds me of you.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: It's attractive.

jokes.text: Ron, this is the Hawaiian god of anger. It reminded us of you when you're at work. A handsome gentleman.
jokes.setup: Leslie is handing out personalized gifts and has one for Ron.
jokes.punchline: She describes a fierce anger deity — which is insulting — and then immediately adds 'A handsome gentleman,' both softening it and making it funnier.
jokes.explanation: A clean character-based joke playing on Ron's legendary workplace intimidation. 'A handsome gentleman' is a smart recovery beat that makes the gift feel both affectionate and accurate. The rhythm of the three-part delivery (description, association, compliment) is well-structured.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Jerry, you got the exact same gifts last year. A luggage tag, a travel pillow, and a book about Paris.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I know! Isn't it great? Now I have two of each!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's not... Jerry, that means you got the same gift twice.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Exactly! What are the odds?

jokes.text: We got Jerry some earbuds, and a bag of peanuts, and the Skymall catalog. Same thing you got me from your trip to Washington!
jokes.setup: Leslie has personalized thoughtful gifts for everyone. She gets to Jerry.
jokes.punchline: Jerry gets airplane freebies — the saddest possible gifts — and then reveals she gave him THE EXACT SAME THINGS from the last trip. Double humiliation.
jokes.explanation: A perfectly constructed Jerry joke. The escalation from 'personalized gifts' to 'airplane freebies' is already great, but Jerry's reveal that this is a repeat offense makes it truly excellent. His delivery of it — with apparent resignation rather than anger — deepens the pathos-comedy blend that defines the Jerry running gag. High character integration score because this only works as a Jerry joke.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I got a photo with my personal hero!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's amazing! Who is it?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Derek Jeter!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, that's Derek Jeter from the reboot of 'Cops,' right?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah! He plays Officer Johnson. The show's only on basic cable but it's incredible.

jokes.text: Tom, we got you an autographed portrait of your personal hero. No way! Scott Caan from Hawaii Five-0!
jokes.setup: 'Personal hero' sets up an expectation of someone impressive or meaningful.
jokes.punchline: Scott Caan — a secondary actor from a CBS procedural — is Tom's hero, perfectly skewering Tom's shallow celebrity obsession.
jokes.explanation: A solid Tom joke. Scott Caan is a perfectly chosen celebrity — not famous enough to be impressive, but specific enough to feel researched. The specificity is what elevates it above a generic 'Tom worships celebrities' joke.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So April asked us to throw something into a volcano, and we did it. No questions asked. That's what friends do.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I appreciate that.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We still don't know what it was.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: And you never will.

jokes.text: April, as requested, we threw that box you gave us into that volcano. Thank you.
jokes.setup: Leslie is listing personalized gifts. April's 'gift' is revealed to be a request she made before they left.
jokes.punchline: April asked them to throw an unspecified box into a volcano. No explanation. April's single-word 'Thank you' is the perfect button.
jokes.explanation: This is the strongest joke in the gifts sequence. The economy is exceptional — we never learn what's in the box, which is the right choice. The joke is entirely in the implication: April has sinister/strange enough reasons to need a box thrown into a volcano that Leslie and Ben just... did it. And April's deadpan 'Thank you' is one of the best character buttons in the scene. Pure April Ludgate. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I haven't showered in three days. I'm not trying to be gross, I just haven't had time.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Andy, we're on our honeymoon.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I know, and it's great. But I've been having so much fun, I just haven't gotten around to it. Plus, I read somewhere that if you don't shower for a while, your body adjusts and you don't smell as bad.

jokes.text: Andy, as you requested, got you a three-pack of white T-shirts from Target. Thank you. All mine are dirty.
jokes.setup: After April's absurdist volcano request, Andy's honeymoon request is revealed.
jokes.punchline: A three-pack of T-shirts from Target — the most mundane possible ask — because all his are dirty. No ambition, no mystery. Just Andy.
jokes.explanation: The contrast with April's dark mystery box makes this even funnier. April has unknowable sinister needs; Andy just needs clean shirts. 'All mine are dirty' as a matter-of-fact explanation is the perfect Andy button — he has no self-awareness about how low-effort his request is.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: The Pawnee Sun is not just a newspaper, it's a institution. A pillar of our community. Sure, it has some typos, and yes, sometimes the ink comes off on your hands, and okay, the sports section is just box scores with no analysis, but it's OURS. We should be proud of it!

jokes.text: There's so many wonderful, talented journalists here. Also here are some reporters from the Pawnee Sun.
jokes.setup: Leslie opens by complimenting the journalists in the room.
jokes.punchline: 'Also here are some reporters from the Pawnee Sun' — they are excluded from the compliment, positioned as lesser beings.
jokes.explanation: A classic roast structure executed cleanly. The 'also here are' construction is a well-worn comedic device but it's deployed with good timing and the local specificity (Pawnee Sun) grounds it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm going to describe something that sounds absolutely horrific, but then say 'It's all in good fun' and everyone will laugh because the contrast is so absurd.

jokes.text: Some people say that it's a useless tabloid. But I don't think it's useless. I think it's great for housebreaking puppies.
jokes.setup: Leslie seems to defend the Pawnee Sun against critics.
jokes.punchline: The defense is actually a deeper insult — the newspaper is only useful as dog training material.
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection structure. The fake defense followed by a buried insult is a solid roast move. The specific image of housebreaking puppies is vivid and slightly mean in the right way. Loses some points because this joke will be stolen and repurposed as a callback, which retroactively makes this the setup for a bigger laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have a joke for the roast.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh, Ron, you don't have to—

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: A government official walks into a bar. The bartender says, 'What'll it be?' The official says, 'I'll have a drink that was processed with zero bureaucratic overhead and delivered on time.' The bartender looks confused and says, 'That's impossible.' The official replies, 'I know. That's the joke.'

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron... that's not really a joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: It's hilarious. Efficient government. Inherently funny.

jokes.text: 364 days a year, they rake me over the coals. Today, I take those burning coals, I shove them back down their throats, and I watch their melting flesh drip off their worthless faces!
jokes.setup: Leslie is in a talking head explaining the roast event as playful.
jokes.punchline: Her description of retaliation escalates from metaphorical to graphic body horror, completely overshooting 'good fun.'
jokes.explanation: A great character moment. Leslie's passionate competitiveness tips into unhinged violent imagery before she snaps back to 'It's all in good fun.' The escalation from burning coals → shoveling them down throats → melting flesh dripping off faces is genuinely surprising and very funny. The snap cut to cheerful 'It's all in good fun' is the perfect button. High character integration: this is Leslie's intensity weaponized comedically.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Hey Ann, you're looking fit today! Have you been working out?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Oh, thanks Chris. Actually, I have to run to a meeting.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: That's the spirit! A morning jog before work? That's exactly the kind of optimized cardio routine I've been recommending to everyone at the office. You're inspiring me right now.

jokes.text: I have a joke for you. The government in this town is excellent and uses your tax dollars efficiently. - That's not really a joke, Ron. - I disagree. I find it hilarious.
jokes.setup: Leslie asks for jokes for her roast speech. Ron offers one.
jokes.punchline: Ron's 'joke' is a sincere-sounding absurdist statement that's only funny if you know he's a libertarian who finds government inefficiency darkly amusing — then insisting it IS hilarious when Leslie pushes back.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Ron Swanson's entire character philosophy compressed into two lines. The joke works on a meta level: his 'joke' IS a joke, but only if you know him. His deadpan insistence that he finds it hilarious is the payoff. Near-perfect character integration — no other character on any show could deliver this beat.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I apologize for entering. The door was open.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I wish it hadn't been.

jokes.text: Ann Perkins! Got to run to a meeting. With Ron. Great idea! I'll run to my next meeting.
jokes.setup: Ann runs into Chris, whom she wants to ask to be her sperm donor. She's nervous and makes up an excuse to leave.
jokes.punchline: Chris, oblivious and relentlessly positive, responds to her abrupt escape with genuine enthusiasm and mirrors it.
jokes.explanation: A light cringe beat that works because of Chris's character — his inability to register awkwardness and his reflexive positivity turns Ann's nervous escape into an inadvertent bonding moment. Functional but not memorable.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I need a greeting card that says 'I'm sorry I ruined your life, but not in a permanent way, and also I made a decent lasagna.'

jokes.text: Turns out they don't make greeting cards for asking your ex-boyfriend if he will artificially inseminate you.
jokes.setup: Ann explains in a talking head why she can't work up the nerve to ask Chris to be her sperm donor.
jokes.punchline: She frames the problem as a Hallmark gap — there's no card for this — which is both an absurd observation and a perfect encapsulation of her overthinking.
jokes.explanation: A genuinely funny, quotable line. The greeting card framing is an original way to frame a very specific social awkwardness. High economy — the joke does a lot of work efficiently. Would score higher if Ann's character were more distinctly integrated, but the line would work from several characters.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Ron, I need to ask you something. How do I ask a friend to... help me make a baby?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Just ask them directly.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Okay, so I've been thinking about asking Ben to be my... sperm donor.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That's not a euphemism, Ann.

jokes.text: I want my friend to do something for me, and I don't know how to ask him. What do you want him to do? Plant ficuses. In my front yard.
jokes.setup: Ann asks Ron for advice about being blunt and direct, framing her actual request (sperm donation) as a metaphor.
jokes.punchline: Her metaphor is 'plant ficuses in my front yard' — the grossest, most strained euphemism possible, which Ron immediately spots.
jokes.explanation: The setup is good — Ann's inability to be direct leads her to the world's most transparent euphemism. The cringe of both the metaphor choice AND Ron immediately seeing through it creates a nice two-layer joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You need to till the soil, break it up real good. Work it with your hands until it's soft and moist.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Then you just... push your seed in, real deep, and really get it in there.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Once you've got your seed planted, you gotta water it every single day and make sure it gets plenty of attention.

jokes.text: Grossest metaphor ever. I've seen your house. You'd have more success if he planted ficuses in your backyard.
jokes.setup: Ron sees through Ann's 'planting ficuses' metaphor for asking Chris to be her sperm donor.
jokes.punchline: Ron, in full deadpan, not only calls out that it's the 'grossest metaphor ever' but extends the metaphor in a cruder anatomical direction with calm pragmatism.
jokes.explanation: Ron Swanson at his best: he acknowledges the subtext, dismisses the euphemism, and offers blunt practical advice all simultaneously — in two sentences. 'I've seen your house' as a grounding detail before the anatomical pivot is brilliant economy. Near-perfect character integration: only Ron would reframe artificial insemination as a landscaping logistics question.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You need to stop trying to have a baby by yourself. It's not going to work.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I know that now.

jokes.text: 'I wish that were possible.' — Ann's response when Ron tells her to 'plant the damn ficuses yourself.'
jokes.setup: Ron bluntly tells Ann to just handle her situation herself; she responds in the metaphor.
jokes.punchline: 'I wish that were possible' — Ann maintains the ficus metaphor while acknowledging the biological limitation, which is both the correct and the most awkward possible response.
jokes.explanation: A tight, economical callback within the same scene. The joke works because Ann accidentally makes the situation even more explicit by staying in metaphor. Ron's likely expression (inferred) would be the button.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: This is beautiful. Who's the artist?

dialogue.speaker: Jessica
dialogue.line: My late husband painted it.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Oh, I'm so sorry for your loss.

dialogue.speaker: Jessica
dialogue.line: Don't be. He was a terrible painter.

jokes.text: Win-win. Except for the rain forest.
jokes.setup: Ben says running the charity is a 'win-win.'
jokes.punchline: He immediately qualifies it with 'Except for the rain forest' — acknowledging the environmental cost of the office's excess.
jokes.explanation: A clean callback button that lands well. The economy is exceptional — three words deliver the entire punchline. Slight overlap with joke 18 as it's essentially the same bit's button rather than a new comedic idea.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: The best part about working for a non-profit is knowing that your work directly helps the community. Sure, we had to clear-cut an old-growth forest to build our new office furniture, but that's a small price to pay for the greater good.

jokes.text: There's even a rumor going around that the chocolate is made of rat parts. Well... You know what they say about rumors. They're mostly true. Including the rat thing? Yeah. What are you gonna do? It's where all the flavor comes from.
jokes.setup: Newport mentions a PR crisis — a rumor that Sweetums chocolate contains rat parts.
jokes.punchline: Newport confirms the rumor is true, then escalates to 'It's where all the flavor comes from' — delivered with complete calm.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully structured dark comedy beat. The escalation through three responses — yes it's true → so what → it's the SECRET INGREDIENT — is perfectly paced. 'It's where all the flavor comes from' is a genuinely great line: casually proud, completely amoral, and absurdly logical. High quotability. The 'what are you gonna do' shrug before the reveal is excellent structural economy.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: So the rumors about Sweetums chocolate... are they true? Like, the whole thing about rat parts?

dialogue.speaker: Jessica
dialogue.line: Yeah, pretty much. I mean, not like whole rats or anything, but yeah, there's definitely rat in there. It's mostly rat.

jokes.text: Oh, would you look at that. There is a smudge on my tail. [Wipes tail on Ben's jacket] All better.
jokes.setup: Right after casually confirming rat parts are in the chocolate, Newport notices something on his tail.
jokes.punchline: Newport (implied to be a large Sweetums mascot character in a costume) wipes his tail on Ben's jacket with no acknowledgment of the inappropriateness, then declares it 'All better.'
jokes.explanation: A physical/visual comedy beat that works well. The absurdity of the costume character's total lack of self-awareness, combined with the timing immediately after the rat parts revelation, creates a surreal comedic moment. 'All better' is a great button. Rewatch bonus because the physical execution likely adds a lot.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Wait, so there were rat parts in the food?

dialogue.speaker: Jessica
dialogue.line: Yeah, but only a little bit. The health inspector said it was within acceptable levels.

jokes.text: Oh well, well, well. If it isn't Kim Terlando from the Pawnee Sun. Do you happen to have a can opener? 'Cause I'm about to open this on you. [holds up can of whoop ass] Did you make that can of 'whoop ass' for this exact moment?
jokes.setup: Leslie runs into her rival journalist Kim before the roast.
jokes.punchline: Leslie has literally brought a prop can labeled 'whoop ass' — the idiom made physical — and Kim instantly calls her out for the prep work involved.
jokes.explanation: Making the idiom literal is a classic comedy move, but the execution is good — Leslie's level of preparation is itself part of the joke, and Kim's immediate recognition ('Did you make that?') gives it a second comedic layer. Becomes more important as a setup for the callback when Leslie is forced to 'open it on herself.'

dialogue.line: The implication that she literally has a tail that she grooms

jokes.text: I think I accidentally got the meat option. Yeah, and I got the veggie option. Shauna Malwae-Tweep, my ex-girlfriend.
jokes.setup: Chris has an awkward run-in with his ex-girlfriend Shauna at the event.
jokes.punchline: The 'mix-em-up' of food orders is the mundane thing filling the space of a far more complex emotional situation — and Chris's talking head aside ('my ex-girlfriend') arrives with characteristic deadpan understatement.
jokes.explanation: A light comedic beat that works more as scene-setting than as a proper joke. The food order mix-up as an icebreaker for an awkward ex-encounter is relatable but not especially original. Chris's aside is the best moment in the beat.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.line: His defensive disclaimer delivered as if it's a punchline

jokes.text: Whoa! Check out the new digs. - Pass. - You came down here to pass on helping me? - Yeah, I wanted to see what your face looked like when I said no. It was totally worth it.
jokes.setup: Ben needs help at his new job. Tom and Andy come to see the office.
jokes.punchline: Tom admits he came specifically to watch Ben's face fall when he refuses. The self-awareness of this admission is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Tom at his most honest and most Tom. The logic of traveling somewhere just to watch someone's disappointment face is absurd but utterly in character. 'It was totally worth it' is a perfectly satisfied button.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I have this great joke about a can opener. So this guy walks into a bar with a can opener...

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And he sits down and orders a drink, and the bartender says, 'Hey, why do you have that can opener?' And he says, 'Well, I use it to open cans!'

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So anyway, the punchline is— *pulls out an actual can opener from her bag* —I made this prop!

jokes.text: It's just that life is pointless and nothing matters and I'm always tired. Also, I can't sleep, I'm overeating, none of my old hobbies interest me.
jokes.setup: Asked if he's okay, Andy cheerfully lists his symptoms.
jokes.punchline: He describes clinical depression with complete absence of insight or alarm — the 'fine' at the start makes everything that follows more alarming and funnier.
jokes.explanation: Works on a dark comedy level — Andy is describing textbook depression with zero awareness that it's serious. The list structure (building from 'life is pointless' to mundane symptoms) is well-paced. High character integration because Andy's obliviousness is the entire joke.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This speech is so powerful, it should come with a warning label.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Actually, it does. I put one on there myself.

jokes.text: Ever since Andy failed the police academy exam, his self-esteem has hit rock bottom. He's always sad and sweaty. He's usually happy and sweaty.
jokes.setup: April explains Andy's emotional state in a talking head.
jokes.punchline: The distinction she draws is not that he's sad but that the SWEATY is constant — the sadness is the anomaly. 'Usually happy and sweaty' is the specific detail that makes it an April joke.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional economy and character integration. April's love for Andy expressed through the most matter-of-fact, slightly gross observation is very on-brand. The pivot — 'He's always sad and sweaty / He's usually happy and sweaty' — lands the joke in the contrast. 'Usually happy and sweaty' is a genuinely quotable description of Andy Dwyer.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Everyone, I'd like you to meet my ex-girlfriend. We dated for three years. It ended amicably. She's a wonderful person. We just wanted different things.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Anyway, one time at Applebee's, the waiter brought her a plate of mozzarella sticks instead of her quesadilla, and she just... ate them. Didn't say anything. Just ate the whole plate.

jokes.text: Well, they bring me fancy lunches here. If you stay, you can have some. What? Crab, caviar? On behalf of Tommy's Tummy Foundation, I'm happy to accept this generous donation.
jokes.setup: Tom was about to leave until he hears there's free fancy food.
jokes.punchline: Tom instantly pivots and reframes staying for crab and caviar as an official charitable act.
jokes.explanation: A quick callback that extends the Tommy's Tummy Foundation bit well. The official charitable framing of eating free food is funny. Somewhat dependent on the setup joke for its impact.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Wait, you came all the way here just to say no?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Yes. I wanted to see the look on your face when you realized I wasn't going to help you.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's... that's really mean.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I know. It was great.

jokes.text: It's nice to be here among all of these excellent journalists. And also the people that work with me over at the Pawnee Sun. Damn it. That was my opener.
jokes.setup: Kim Terlando takes the podium and uses the same exact opener Leslie had prepared.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's horrified 'Damn it. That was my opener.' confirms the speech has been stolen, and the joke has a meta layer — the audience has already heard this joke, making the theft immediately obvious.
jokes.explanation: Structurally brilliant. The callback here is layered: the in-episode callback (Kim stealing Leslie's joke), the meta callback (the audience recognizing it), and Leslie's immediate reaction all land simultaneously. The structure is essentially perfect — setup the joke, show it getting stolen, let the victim react. The 9.0 structure score is justified because the writers engineered this entire sequence as a callback delivery mechanism. One of the episode's strongest moments.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm fine! Why wouldn't I be? I've got plenty of energy, I'm sleeping great, food tastes amazing, I love going outside, I'm optimistic about the future, I laugh at jokes, I care about stuff, I shower regularly, and I have a strong will to live.

jokes.text: Jerry, stop laughing. Those are stolen jokes! Totally dead. What am I gonna do? Oh! I just opened up a can of 'whoop ass' on myself!
jokes.setup: All of Leslie's jokes have been stolen and delivered by Kim. Leslie is in crisis.
jokes.punchline: Leslie realizes the prop can of whoop ass she prepared to use on Kim has now been used on herself — the setup from joke 22 fully inverted.
jokes.explanation: A masterful callback payoff. The can-of-whoop-ass prop was set up for this exact reversal, and it lands perfectly. Leslie's dawning horror as she arrives at this conclusion is a great character moment, and the line itself is quotable and punchy. The callback structure is clean and the emotional stakes (Leslie's humiliation) give it genuine comedic weight.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Andy's not depressed anymore. He's just... naturally like this.

jokes.text: I remember the very first Correspondents' Lunch. I rode here in a horse and buggy. No, no, no, that wasn't a joke. I actually did. That also was not a joke.
jokes.setup: The elderly Councilman Milton attempts to contribute to the roast.
jokes.punchline: He matter-of-factly insists his historical detail is not comedic — which is itself funny — then has to clarify a second time that the clarification also isn't a joke.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed old-person joke that avoids cliché. The double-clarification structure ('that wasn't a joke / that also was not a joke') escalates the comedy while maintaining his total seriousness. The comedy is in the content (he's so old he rode a buggy) AND the structure (he has to explain himself twice). Very efficient.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You know what, I appreciate what you all are doing here, but I gotta bounce. I have my own charity work I need to get to.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, it's called 'feeding Tom Haverford,' and it's a very worthy cause.

jokes.text: Councilman Milton is old, right? And he's wearing a green tie. So, like, maybe there's something there, where, like, he went to school with his high-school buddies that were dinosaurs. And his tie is green. They're green.
jokes.setup: Ann is asked to contribute jokes for Leslie's new speech.
jokes.punchline: Ann's pitch is spectacularly bad — the joke has no logic, the callback to 'his tie is green / they're green' explains nothing, and the whole thing collapses into helpless confusion.
jokes.explanation: The joke-about-a-bad-joke genre. Ann's pitch is deliberately terrible, and the deliberate terribleness is well-calibrated — it follows a recognizable joke structure (observation → connection → payoff) but the connection is non-existent. 'They're green' as the 'punchline' is a great specific choice. The comedy is in watching someone try and catastrophically fail.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait. No. Is she... is she telling my jokes?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's my bit about the raccoons. That's MY bit!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God. Oh my God, she stole that one too. And that one.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: She's using everything. The thing about the Parks Department budget? The funny voice I do? All of it!

jokes.text: Oh, Ann, you're too beautiful to be funny. It's not your fault. You've never had to compensate for anything. The rest of you ugly nerds need to give me some jokes stat.
jokes.setup: Ann delivers a terrible joke pitch. Leslie responds.
jokes.punchline: Leslie dismisses Ann with a backhanded compliment — 'too beautiful to be funny' — then pivots to insulting everyone else as 'ugly nerds,' which is both harsh and warm.
jokes.explanation: A great Leslie Knope speech. The theory that beautiful people don't develop comedic skills because they don't need to is both absurd and surprisingly arguable — it has the shape of wisdom. Then pivoting to call the writers 'ugly nerds' while asking them for help is both insulting and affectionate. High character integration: this is Leslie's specific brand of chaotic-but-loving management.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, what are you doing with that?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: You started it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's not fair! I was just trying to—

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Shhh. Shhh.

jokes.text: It's the Redwood Music Program. It's an after-school music class for at-risk kids. It'll keep them off the street. And the streets, as you know, are dangerous. Example -- I fell in a sewer grate once. I was there all day. In conclusion, we cannot let our children live in the sewer any longer.
jokes.setup: Andy finds a charity and presents it to Ben and April.
jokes.punchline: His pitch starts legitimately, then pivots to personal anecdote (he fell in a sewer), and concludes with a non-sequitur moral about keeping children out of sewers — a problem the music program does not address.
jokes.explanation: Andy's presentation style — starting earnest, derailing via personal trauma, and concluding with a completely off-topic call to action — is pitch-perfect character comedy. 'I was there all day' and 'we cannot let our children live in the sewer any longer' are great specific lines. Maximum character integration: only Andy would pitch a music program with a sewer grate anecdote.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.line: I'm so old, I remember when Parks and Recreation first aired.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.line: No, I'm serious. I'm literally that old. I was there. I watched it live.

jokes.text: Um, yeah. I got a good one. It's called the Clean Sheet Foundation. That's my pick. They provide legal assistance to the KKK.
jokes.setup: Ben asks for other charity pitches after Andy's. Tom says he has a good one.
jokes.punchline: The 'Clean Sheet Foundation' sounds legitimate until Tom reveals it provides legal assistance to the KKK — the name is a horrifying pun in retrospect.
jokes.explanation: A dark, well-constructed joke. The 'Clean Sheet Foundation' is a clever name-as-pun that only registers after the reveal. The economy is excellent — the reveal is perfectly timed. Loses character integration points because Tom nominating a KKK charity is wildly out of character even for Tom, making this feel more like a writer's room joke than a Tom joke. The 'can you pass the bonbons' follow-up adds a great layer of casual obliviousness.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Jerry, you need to sit in the corner and think about what you've done.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Leslie, I'm 60 years old.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And you're acting like you're six. Corner. Now.

jokes.text: Can you pass the bonbons?
jokes.setup: Tom has just nominated a charity that provides legal assistance to the KKK.
jokes.punchline: His immediate follow-up is asking for bonbons — total indifference to the horror of his suggestion.
jokes.explanation: A masterclass in comedic economy. Three words that completely define Tom's character in this moment: he has no idea what he's done, or doesn't care, and wants luxury snacks immediately. The contrast between the severity of what he just said and the casualness of the bonbon request is the entire joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Okay, here's one: Why did the old man wear green? Because he was old!

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Get it? Old... green... together?

jokes.text: Perd Hapley is here today. Or, as Perd would say, 'My name is Perd Hapley, and the person I see here today... is me.'
jokes.setup: Leslie previews a joke about Perd Hapley, the local news anchor known for stating the obvious at length.
jokes.punchline: The Perd impression captures his verbal tic perfectly — he introduces himself via an elaborate tautology about seeing himself.
jokes.explanation: A well-executed Perd impression that captures his character precisely. The circular tautology ('the person I see here today is me') is a good parody of his style. Works best for viewers who know the character.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, no, no. I have a theory about beautiful people. Since they never have to develop a sense of humor, they never do. It's like how birds don't have a sense of smell.

jokes.text: Everyone seems to be laughing now. Do you see what is happening with Chris and Shauna? They are flirting like crazy. It's disgusting. They're in public. - That's called a conversation. -Ron.
jokes.setup: Perd narrates events like a news anchor; Ron dismisses Leslie's romantic jealousy with one word.
jokes.punchline: Ron's single-word 'Ron' — delivered after Leslie desperately asserts 'There are no ficuses' — functions as 'I know exactly what's happening and I want no part of it.' Perd Hapley narrating 'everyone seems to be laughing now' as it's happening is also a great touch.
jokes.explanation: A multi-layer comedic beat. Perd's literal news-anchor narration of events happening in real time is a reliable gag, and Ron's withdrawal from the ficuses conversation is a good reaction beat. A bit scattered as a single joke.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Look, I learned clarinet in high school, and it changed my life. Music programs are essential for kids.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Without them, where are these kids gonna go? The sewers? We can't have children living in the sewers.

jokes.text: Maybe I should just do impressions. 'I'm-a Borat.' There's one. But I need to do someone that no one has heard before. Like, I don't know, Neve Campbell? What does Neve Campbell sound like? I don't know. Someone fucking tell me what Neve Campbell sounds like.
jokes.setup: Leslie is in crisis mode trying to improvise new speech material.
jokes.punchline: Her spiral from 'Borat impression' to 'Neve Campbell impression' (an actress with no distinctive voice) to a desperate demand for information is a great comedic unraveling.
jokes.explanation: Leslie's panicked logic — impressions are a fallback, Borat is too well-known, let's pick someone obscure like Neve Campbell — is both perfectly characterful and absurdly funny. 'Someone fucking tell me what Neve Campbell sounds like' is the best escalation button. The joke works because it follows actual improv-comedy logic (be original!) taken to an insane conclusion. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I think we should help the KKK.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: The Kids Kickball Klassic. By the way, does anyone have any candy?

jokes.text: 'Strap on your adult diapers, everyone. Because you're about to wet yourself from laughter. Give it up for Leslie Knope.'
jokes.setup: Leslie prepared a grandiose introduction for herself to be read before her speech.
jokes.punchline: The introduction she wrote promises the speech will be so funny people will wet themselves — which sets up the subsequent catastrophic failure perfectly.
jokes.explanation: A well-engineered setup for disaster. Leslie writing her own over-the-top introduction ('adult diapers') is perfect hubris before the fall. The rewatch bonus is significant because knowing what follows makes this introduction darkly hilarious on second viewing.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And this is my Perd Hapley impression: 'The thing about this thing is that this thing is a thing. And that thing? Also a thing.'

jokes.text: 'Whassup,' Pawnee? Um... Borat.
jokes.setup: Leslie takes the stage to deliver her emergency backup speech after all her material was stolen.
jokes.punchline: Her entire speech is: a dated 'Whassup' reference, a pause, and then a single word Borat impression with no content. Then she immediately claims they're giving her the light to leave.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The beautiful payoff to the Neve Campbell/Borat spiral: Leslie goes with Borat. And her entire speech is two words and a pause. The economy is perfect — 10.0 because the joke IS the absence of content. 'Whassup' then 'Borat' then walking off is a masterpiece of comedic structure built on Leslie's total breakdown. The callback to the Borat conversation makes it even better. High character integration: only Leslie would experience this as a complete performance.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Chris and Shauna seem really close.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That's called being friends, Ann. It's a normal thing that happens between people.

jokes.text: Tom, do you have to run that right now? Oh, no, Ben! These smoothies will just blend themselves!
jokes.setup: Ben asks Tom to stop running something (implied: a blender) at an inconvenient moment.
jokes.punchline: Tom's outraged sarcasm — 'These smoothies will just blend themselves!' — treats luxury self-care as an urgent professional obligation.
jokes.explanation: A good Tom character beat. The sarcasm ('will just blend themselves') treating smoothie-making as an urgent professional necessity is very Tom. Slightly undercut by being a brief transitional joke rather than a fully developed bit.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Ron, I need to tell you the truth about my metaphor. When I said I was a 'bird with a broken wing,' I wasn't being poetic. I was literally talking about the time I hit a pigeon with my car.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You... you've been speaking about vehicular bird assault this entire time?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Yes.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Ann, I have spent the last three weeks consoling you about your metaphorical struggles. I wrote you a seventeen-page memo on resilience. I even cried, Ann. I cried.

jokes.text: Well, I'm terribly disappointed. But I'm sure the doctors or giraffes or whatever you decided to help will be thrilled with the whatever you decided to whatever.
jokes.setup: Ben's charity has gone to the Rural Ambu-care ambulance project instead of Andy's music program.
jokes.punchline: Tom's response to the disappointment is a sentence that progressively gives up — 'doctors or giraffes or whatever' and 'the whatever you decided to whatever' collapses into complete verbal surrender.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully written sentence that deliberately falls apart. Tom's inability to care about anything outside his comfort zone expressed through a grammatical breakdown is funny and original. 'Doctors or giraffes or whatever' is particularly good — the range from plausible to absurd in three words. 'The whatever you decided to whatever' is the best kind of comedy-through-collapse.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: I need new material. Let me try something edgy. You know who I can do? That guy from that one movie... what's his name... anyway, screw it, I give up on impressions!

jokes.text: 'Chris-toe-fur.' It's like you have furry toes. Hilarious.
jokes.setup: Ann is trying to approach Chris, observed by Perd Hapley who is narrating everything.
jokes.punchline: Perd introduces himself by riffing on 'Christopher' — breaking down the name to note it contains 'fur' — and finds it hilarious. No one else does.
jokes.explanation: A great Perd Hapley joke. The wordplay is terrible-on-purpose and Perd's self-congratulation ('Hilarious') makes it funnier. Perfect character integration — Perd is always insufferably pleased with his own verbal observations. The 'furry toes' etymology is exactly the right level of bad.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.line: Leslie Knope is a tireless public servant who has dedicated her life to making Pawnee a better place. She is widely regarded as the most competent civil servant in the history of local government. Some say she's smarter than any Harvard graduate, and her organizational skills are unmatched. She has never made a mistake in her professional career. Leslie Knope: American hero.

jokes.text: I have a question for you. It's something very important. Which is... What is your spirit animal?
jokes.setup: Ann has built up to asking Chris a very important question — we assume she's about to ask him to be her sperm donor.
jokes.punchline: She chickens out and asks about his spirit animal instead.
jokes.explanation: A standard misdirection-via-chickening-out beat. The setup (something very important) makes the pivot (spirit animal) land well. The anticipation created by the long pause and buildup amplifies the deflation. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I did great out there!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, you died up there.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, I killed! The crowd loved me!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You were booed off stage.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: They were cheering! I'm a natural performer!

jokes.text: Jaguar. Why do you ask? Doin' a survey. Well, survey completed. So take 'er easy. Uh, you didn't ask me. But if you had, the answer I would have given is... Doggie.
jokes.setup: Chris answers Ann's spirit animal question, then Ann exits. Perd has been listening.
jokes.punchline: Perd volunteers his own spirit animal ('Doggie') despite not being asked, with complete seriousness and a formal grammatical construction ('the answer I would have given is').
jokes.explanation: Perd Hapley at his best. The elaborate formal phrasing ('the answer I would have given is...') deployed for the word 'Doggie' is a perfect Perd joke. His intrusion into a private conversation with complete obliviousness is spot-on. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Tom, you need to stop using the blender at work.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh, I'm sorry, should I just blend myself into a smoothie instead?

jokes.text: Chris, Ann wants to ask you something right now. Go, Ann. - In front of Perd? - Yes. No more delays. Go.
jokes.setup: Ron has had enough of Ann's delays and forces the conversation.
jokes.punchline: Ann's horror at having to do it in front of Perd — a local news anchor who is literally narrating events — and Ron's complete indifference to this concern.
jokes.explanation: A good escalation of the cringe plot. Ron forcing the conversation despite (or because of) Perd's presence is funny, and 'No more delays. Go.' is a great Ron Swanson command. The presence of Perd makes it significantly funnier than it would be otherwise.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Why would I donate to an ambulance charity? If I'm dying, I don't want to be saved. I want to stay dead.

jokes.text: I want to have a baby. Will you be the sperm donor? The story of this situation is it's extremely personal. Think it over. Bye.
jokes.setup: Ann finally asks Chris — in front of Perd Hapley — to be her sperm donor.
jokes.punchline: Perd's immediate reaction is to announce to no one in particular that this is 'extremely personal' and then cheerfully sign off.
jokes.explanation: Perd Hapley at peak Perd. He narrates the emotional weight of the scene ('extremely personal'), validates it, and then professionally exits the conversation as if filing a report. 'Think it over. Bye.' is a perfect button — the 'bye' especially, as if he's wrapping up a segment. Maximum character integration. The joke is built entirely on Perd's complete inability to have a human reaction.

dialogue.speaker: Jessica
dialogue.line: I'm leaving. And honestly, I don't care about the charity, the decision, any of it. I'm going home to watch TV, eat some nachos, maybe sleep for three days straight. Or don't sleep. Who cares? Not me.

jokes.text: Leslie, permission to leave the corner. Denied. But, look, I did not lose your speech after all. I forgot. I put it in my shoe for safekeeping. It's a little moist, but it is still here.
jokes.setup: Jerry was sent to a corner as punishment. He comes back with news.
jokes.punchline: Jerry put the speech in his shoe 'for safekeeping.' The speech is moist. He has just revealed the source of the entire episode's crisis was his shoe.
jokes.explanation: A great Jerry joke with real structural payoff. Jerry's solution to keeping the speech safe was to put it in his shoe — which is not safe, it's the worst possible place, and now it's moist. 'It's a little moist' delivered as a qualifier is the best word in the joke. The realization that this is why Kim got the speech (somehow) while Jerry's shoe had it is a classic Jerry-causes-disaster beat.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Hey Chris, I've got a joke for you. What do you call a Chris who's really good at his job?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Chris-cellent!

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Oh my god, I'm so funny.

jokes.text: The Pawnee Sun has been one step ahead of me for months. They knew Kernston's withdrew its sponsorship before I even announced it. They asked about the sewage eruption in Ramsett Park right after Ron emailed me. And Kim asked me if I liked the first season of Army Wives just moments after Netflix did.
jokes.setup: Leslie pieces together that her email has been hacked by listing suspicious incidents.
jokes.punchline: The evidence escalates from plausibly sinister (advance knowledge of sponsorship) to slightly suspicious (sewage eruption timing) to completely absurd (Army Wives recommendation timing).
jokes.explanation: A well-structured escalation list. The comedy is in the third item — 'Army Wives recommendations' as evidence of hacking is a great anticlimax that simultaneously characterizes Leslie perfectly. The structure (serious, serious, absurd) is classic comedy list construction.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: So, um, Chris... do you have a spirit animal?

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: A spirit animal? Ann, that's a deeply personal and culturally significant concept. Mine is the Orca Whale — intelligent, powerful, graceful, and an apex predator.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Cool, cool. Great. Well, I'm gonna go... literally anywhere else.

jokes.text: The Pawnee Sun hacked my email. Wait — they knew about Kernston's withdrew sponsorship, asked about the sewage eruption right after Ron emailed, and Kim asked if I liked Army Wives right after Netflix did.
jokes.setup: Leslie pieces together a pattern of suspicious Pawnee Sun knowledge about her private affairs.
jokes.punchline: The escalating list of evidence builds to the absurd final item: Kim knowing Leslie's Netflix activity — making the hacking revelation personal in the most mundane way possible.
jokes.explanation: The escalating evidence list is well-constructed, and the Army Wives Netflix detail is the perfect anticlimax — the hacking was used not just for political intelligence but to monitor Leslie's streaming habits. Shows the all-encompassing nature of the breach through a comedic lens.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Chris, I need to tell you something. I'm in love with you.

dialogue.speaker: Perd
dialogue.line: What we're witnessing here is a woman expressing romantic feelings toward a man. That's a declaration of love.

jokes.text: There is nothing more disgusting than an invasion of privacy. And I should know. I've had many women steal my undershirts.
jokes.setup: Ron sympathizes with Leslie being hacked by invoking his own privacy invasion experience.
jokes.punchline: Ron's privacy violations involve women stealing his undershirts — a bizarre and oddly specific problem that implies a lot about his romantic history.
jokes.explanation: A great Ron Swanson non-sequitur that implies an entire untold backstory. 'Many women' and 'undershirts' specifically — not shirts, undershirts — is the perfect Ron detail. The word 'many' does a lot of work, suggesting an ongoing pattern. High character integration: this anecdote makes complete sense for Ron while revealing nothing and everything simultaneously.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait a minute. The Sun knows about the proposal? How would they know that? Nobody knows about that except... oh my God. Oh my God, no. I've been hacked. I've been hacked!

jokes.text: You can't hack into a typewriter. That's all I have to say.
jokes.setup: Leslie is panicking about being hacked and needs to protect her emails.
jokes.punchline: Ron's solution is simply to not use email — typewriters are unhackable.
jokes.explanation: A near-perfect Ron Swanson line. Maximum economy: the entire joke and his philosophy are in nine words. 'That's all I have to say' is a great button — he's not being funny, he's being entirely serious, which IS the joke. High quotability because it's usable in many contexts. One of the most quotable lines in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm going to smash this phone!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Please don't. That's a county phone, and I'm going to have to fill out so much paperwork.

jokes.text: Can it, Unabomber. This is an emergency.
jokes.setup: Ron suggests using a typewriter instead of email to avoid hacking.
jokes.punchline: Leslie calls Ron 'Unabomber' for his anti-technology stance — technically not a fair comparison, but delivered with Leslie's signature urgency.
jokes.explanation: A quick, punchy comeback. 'Unabomber' is an unexpected and slightly wrong comparison (he's anti-tech, not mailing bombs), which makes it funnier. Leslie's total dismissal of a reasonable suggestion is in character. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't appreciate my privacy being invaded. It's a violation of my rights as an American citizen.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Although, I will say, women do tend to steal my clothing. I suppose when you're as attractive as I am, it's just something you have to accept.

jokes.text: There's a 'Top Ten Ben's Butt 2012 slideshow.' You emailed it to Ben and Ann... And The Huffington Post? Yeah, I'm not embarrassed by that.
jokes.setup: Donna is reviewing Leslie's emails to check for embarrassing content that might be used against her.
jokes.punchline: Leslie sent a slideshow rating Ben's butt to a major news outlet, and she's entirely unbothered by this.
jokes.explanation: A great two-stage joke. The escalation from 'emailed Ben and Ann' to 'AND the Huffington Post' is well-timed. Leslie's total lack of shame about the slideshow is the character-specific button. 'I'm not embarrassed by that' delivered without any hesitation is the best delivery choice.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: Email? A government bureaucrat's tool for creating paper trails and documentation. I don't use email.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: If you need to contact me, write it down on a piece of paper, and someone will hand-deliver it to my office. That's how the founders intended communication to work.

jokes.text: Who is Todo Toadfoot? You wrote him an email about riding your dragons to Pelennor Fields and signed it 'Dimple Broadbelt of Buckland.' Yes, that's Ben and my fantasy Lord Of The Rings pen pal letters. I am a little embarrassed by that.
jokes.setup: Donna is finding increasingly embarrassing emails as she reviews Leslie's account.
jokes.punchline: Leslie and Ben have an ongoing Lord of the Rings fantasy pen-pal correspondence — complete with Hobbit names — and Leslie IS embarrassed by this one, unlike the butt slideshow.
jokes.explanation: A wonderful piece of character comedy. The reversal — she's NOT embarrassed by the butt slideshow but IS embarrassed by the LOTR pen pal letters — is funny and character-specific. 'Dimple Broadbelt of Buckland' is a perfectly crafted Hobbit name. Todo Toadfoot as Ben's alias is equally good. The detail that they have an ongoing correspondence is the best part. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, so I was at the store, right? And I had this weird thing happen where my pants were too tight, so I couldn't breathe properly, and then I sharted a little bit.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Why are you telling me this?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Because it's interesting! And then I bought new pants, but they were also too tight, so I went back to the store and I sharted again!

jokes.text: Here's one to me, and it just says 'Thanks.' You're welcome.
jokes.setup: Donna is reviewing emails and finds one sent to herself.
jokes.punchline: The email just says 'Thanks.' Donna's 'You're welcome' — delivered with complete sincerity — is a perfect non-sequitur beat.
jokes.explanation: Beautiful economy — four words total. Donna finding her own email and responding to it in the present tense is a small gem of a joke. 'You're welcome' perfectly characterizes Donna's self-assured response to any acknowledgment.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Leslie, you sent an email to the Associated Press that says 'I love you so much, you make my heart skip a beat.'

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? No, that was supposed to go to Ben!

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Well, it went to the AP instead.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God. Oh my God, no!

jokes.text: Donna: 'Listen, freaky. Every single one of my boyfriends has tried to hack into my email. I've got an idea... Everybody out.'
jokes.setup: The group is panicking about the email hack. Donna suddenly takes charge.
jokes.punchline: Donna has personal expertise in being hacked by boyfriends — an alarming relationship history — and this expert knowledge is what qualifies her to solve the problem.
jokes.explanation: 'Every single one of my boyfriends' implies a long and specific pattern — Donna has dated enough hackers to have developed anti-hacking expertise. Her authority ('Everybody out') emerging from this dark personal history is both funny and characteristically Donna: she's been through some things and has emerged wiser.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Oh wow, here's one from Leslie... 'Dear Ben, I've been thinking about you in your ranger outfit. Meet me at the old ranger station at midnight. I'll be dressed as a sexy forest fire.'

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's not embarrassing, that's just good roleplay.

jokes.text: You are a great specimen.
jokes.setup: Ann is trying to compliment Chris in the context of asking him to father her child.
jokes.punchline: 'Specimen' — the word used in biology labs — as a romantic/personal compliment is immediately, visibly wrong.
jokes.explanation: A cringeworthy word choice that works because Ann is a nurse/medical professional and because she's trying so hard. 'Specimen' instead of 'person' or 'man' captures the clinical awkwardness of the entire sperm-donor conversation perfectly. 'That's a terrible choice of words' as Chris's response is the right button.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Ann, you have great genetics. I mean, your parents did a great job.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Thank you?

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: No, I mean — you're very attractive. Your face is attractive.

jokes.text: Take as much time as you want. Or just maybe, like, a couple days. 'Cause I'm getting antsy. And I'm ovulating on Thursday. So, chop-chop. But take your time. Wear loose pants!
jokes.setup: Ann tells Chris to take his time thinking about the sperm donor request.
jokes.punchline: She immediately qualifies 'take your time' with a specific deadline (Thursday, ovulation), 'chop-chop,' and medical instructions about pants — completely contradicting herself in real-time.
jokes.explanation: Ann's self-contradiction — 'take your time / chop-chop / but take your time / wear loose pants' — is a great comedic unraveling. 'Wear loose pants' as a parting shot is highly quotable and perfectly encapsulates the absurdity of the request. The escalation structure is clean.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Take all the time you need. I'm super casual about this. Like, I don't even care. I'm probably not even going to think about it at all.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Well, maybe I'll think about it a little. But only in a healthy way. Not like, obsessively checking my phone every thirty seconds to see if you texted.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Which I'm not doing, by the way. I'm just... living my life. Super normal. I actually have a lot going on. I've been reading about ovulation cycles and optimal fertility windows, just for fun, as a hobby.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Did you know that a woman's fertility peaks at thirty-five? Wait, no, thirty-two. Actually, I think I read it was twenty-eight. Anyway, I'm just casually learning things!

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: So yeah, no pressure at all. Take your time. A week, a month, whatever. Though my eggs are literally dying as we speak, so...

jokes.text: I gotta tell you, Ron. You were absolutely and totally right. I know. Stop talking and get out. Yep.
jokes.setup: Ann comes to thank Ron for his advice.
jokes.punchline: Ron's response to being told he was right is immediate — 'I know. Stop talking and get out.' He doesn't need validation.
jokes.explanation: Pure Ron. The refusal to accept a thank-you or extended conversation when both parties already know the outcome is perfectly in character. 'Stop talking and get out' is three words that define his entire relationship with small talk. High economy, maximum character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Ron, I just wanted to thank you for your advice. It really helped me.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't recall giving you any advice.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: You don't? You told me to stop trying so hard and just be myself.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That's generic advice that applies to no one. Now if you'll excuse me, I have a woodworking project that requires my attention.

jokes.text: The redneck ambulance is a great choice. We can release a publicity shot of a bucktoothed hayseed taking medicine for the first time in his life.
jokes.setup: Ben announces the charity choice: Rural Ambu-care for underserved rural communities.
jokes.punchline: Newport immediately imagines an exploitative PR strategy using condescending rural stereotypes delivered with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: Newport's casual dehumanization of the charity's beneficiaries — 'bucktoothed hayseed' — is darkly funny. The joke works because it contrasts with Ben's genuine philanthropic intent. Slightly weak on structure — it's more of a character revelation than a proper joke.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm going to tell Kim that there's been a soil contamination issue at the proposed site. It's all fake, of course, but it'll buy us time to figure out what to do.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: By the way, has anyone seen Outbreak? Because that movie is basically a masterclass in how to handle a crisis. Very underrated Jeff Daniels performance.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Anyway, the point is, if Kim thinks there's a contamination problem, she'll have to delay the development while we investigate. Which gives us the upper hand.

jokes.text: Oh, I forgot! It's Fondue Friday. Yay!
jokes.setup: The meeting is wrapping up with serious charity business.
jokes.punchline: Newport suddenly remembers Fondue Friday with uncontained enthusiasm — completely pivoting from charitable work.
jokes.explanation: A light transitional joke. Newport's genuine excitement about fondue immediately after discussing exploitative charity PR is funny but not especially well-crafted. Works as a character beat.

dialogue.speaker: Kim
dialogue.line: I'm not trapped. I've just been too busy with my active sex life to keep up with popular movies.

jokes.text: Get yourself a matching nude portrait? I can call the painter. Please don't.
jokes.setup: Ben says he wants to use some of the saved money on a good idea. Newport guesses wrong.
jokes.punchline: Newport assumes Ben wants another nude portrait — implying there's already one — and is enthusiastic about making it a matched set.
jokes.explanation: A quick visual-joke-implied beat. The implication that there's already a nude portrait of someone in this office, and Newport has the painter on speed-dial, is funny. 'I can call the painter' suggests this is a regular service. Ben's 'Please don't' is the right button.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh yeah? Well I've had way more sexual partners than you. I'm going to need you to write down all of yours so I can make sure I've beaten your number.

jokes.text: First, I'd like you all to check under your chairs. I think you might be surprised and excited by what you find. Is it chocolate? Even better. It's dirt.
jokes.setup: Ben sets up an Oprah-style reveal — 'check under your chairs' — building excited anticipation.
jokes.punchline: It's dirt. Soil samples. The EPA has confirmed minimal acceptable standards.
jokes.explanation: A well-executed misdirection. The Oprah-style reveal structure creates genuine anticipation, Newport's guess ('chocolate?') is reasonable in context, and 'Even better. It's dirt.' is a great deadpan subversion. Ben's genuine excitement about soil samples reaching 'minimal acceptable standards' is excellent character comedy — his enthusiasm for bureaucratic milestones is very Ben.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, so Neve Campbell, right? She was in Party of Five. 'I'm Neve Campbell and I'm in Party of Five.' See, because there's five of them. Five. Party. Of. Five.

jokes.text: So... not too shabby.
jokes.setup: The EPA found 'minimal acceptable standards' in the soil.
jokes.punchline: 'Not too shabby' for barely passing environmental standards for a public park.
jokes.explanation: A small but effective deadpan beat. 'Not too shabby' for barely meeting minimum environmental standards is the right level of understatement. Works as a button for the soil reveal joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I've made a decision about who should get the job. This person is hardworking, dedicated, and has shown real growth.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh wow, Ben's finally announcing it.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: It's obviously Andy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, who are you guys talking about?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Andy, it's you.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Me? I thought you were talking about someone else!

jokes.text: I've also learned that the EPA found midi-chlorians in the soil. How serious is that, exactly? It's very serious, Kim.
jokes.setup: Kim is pressing Leslie at the press conference with a planted fake question.
jokes.punchline: Kim asks about midi-chlorians (a fictional Star Wars concept) and Leslie confirms it's very serious — it's a trap, and Kim just walked into it.
jokes.explanation: The episode's best-constructed plot joke. The midi-chlorian trap is a beautifully layered comedic set piece: Leslie planted the fake email, Kim fell for it and asked about midi-chlorians publicly, Leslie confirmed their seriousness, and then reveals the trap. The choice of midi-chlorians is perfect — Star Wars-specific, immediately recognizable to viewers, and Kim's ignorance is entirely plausible. High earned-vs-cheap score because this payoff was set up through the entire episode's hacking plot.

jokes.text: I really thought you guys would gasp there.
jokes.setup: Leslie dramatically reveals that Kim has been hacking her email — to muted response from the press conference audience.
jokes.punchline: Leslie breaks the fourth wall slightly to note the crowd's underwhelming reaction to what she considers a bombshell.
jokes.explanation: A great meta character beat. Leslie's expectation of a dramatic gasp — and her visible disappointment at not getting one — is a wonderful subversion of press conference drama conventions. 'I really thought you guys would gasp there' is a highly quotable and very Leslie response to underwhelming reactions.

jokes.text: Midi-chlorians are a fictional substance found in the blood of Jedi knights from the movie Star Wars Episode 1: The Phantom Menace. Which, side-note, was a terrible movie. It almost destroyed the franchise, according to my husband. But that is neither here nor there.
jokes.setup: Kim realizes she's been caught in a trap and must now explain why midi-chlorians are fake.
jokes.punchline: She cannot resist adding an editorial opinion about Episode 1 being terrible and 'almost destroying the franchise' — attributed to her husband — before returning to her crisis.
jokes.explanation: The 'side-note' tangent about Episode 1 being terrible is the gold here — Kim is in the middle of professional humiliation and still cannot help herself from editorializing about Star Wars quality. 'According to my husband' is the perfect specificity. Deflects from the trap while being charming and character-specific.

jokes.text: Midi-chlorians are a fictional substance found in the blood of Jedi knights from the movie Star Wars Episode 1: The Phantom Menace. Which, side-note, was a terrible movie. It almost destroyed the franchise, according to my husband. But that is neither here nor there.
jokes.setup: Kim is trying to regain credibility after the midi-chlorian trap. She explains what midi-chlorians are.
jokes.punchline: She cannot resist editorially noting it was a terrible movie — and citing her husband as an authority — while supposedly maintaining journalistic composure.
jokes.explanation: A funny moment of professional breakdown. Kim's attempt to explain herself at a press conference is derailed by her need to editorialize about Episode I. 'According to my husband' as a source is funny. 'But that is neither here nor there' reclaiming professionalism is a good button.

jokes.text: Well... I have never seen Star Wars, because I was too busy hooking up with guys. Unlike you losers. Uh, you wanna compare numbers, Terlando? Get to steppin'.
jokes.setup: Kim is humiliated by not knowing Star Wars and tries to salvage pride by implying she's more sexually active.
jokes.punchline: Leslie immediately accepts the challenge ('you wanna compare numbers?') and dismisses Kim with 'Get to steppin'' — implying she wins this contest too.
jokes.explanation: A great comedic confrontation. Kim's desperate face-saving (never saw Star Wars because too busy with guys) is good, but Leslie's counter — accepting the challenge without missing a beat and dismissing her with 'Get to steppin'' — is excellent. 'Get to steppin'' as Leslie's victory line is highly quotable and shows her confidence. Strong character integration for both characters.

jokes.text: I would just like to point out that Kim Terlando stole all of my jokes for the Pawnee Correspondents' Lunch, and they were great jokes. So I spent the whole night writing new ones. Lucky for you, let's get... started.
jokes.setup: Having defeated Kim, Leslie announces she has new roast material.
jokes.punchline: She builds to 'let's get started' with what sounds like genuine threat — then delivers the Neve Campbell joke.
jokes.explanation: A transitional callback beat that works as a setup for the final gag. 'They were great jokes' is Leslie's self-assessment with no irony, which is very her. 'Lucky for you' building expectation for what turns out to be a Neve Campbell joke is the real joke here.

jokes.text: You know who else is excited to be here? Neve Campbell. What a great party... of five.
jokes.setup: Leslie has spent the episode desperately researching what Neve Campbell sounds like, ultimately having no material.
jokes.punchline: Her 'new' Neve Campbell material is a Party of Five pun — the show Campbell starred in — which is the lamest possible use of the impression prep.
jokes.explanation: A satisfying callback to the Neve Campbell obsession. The pun ('party... of five') is deliberately groan-worthy and the pause before 'of five' is a great delivery beat. The joke is meta: Leslie researched Neve Campbell all episode and her payoff is a TV show title pun. The episode appreciates the lameness and so does the audience.

jokes.text: That guy? Do you even know him? Oh, my God, Andy, it's you.
jokes.setup: Ben has been setting up a dramatic reveal of who will be his new assistant at the Sweetums Foundation. He says the person is 'sitting right here in this courtyard.'
jokes.punchline: Andy looks at a random stranger, then realizes Ben means him.
jokes.explanation: A classic Andy moment. His first instinct is to look at a stranger rather than consider that it might be himself. The beat is earned by Andy's established low self-esteem from the police academy failure. 'Do you even know him?' is a great suspicious aside. The format is familiar but executed well.

jokes.text: Uh-oh. What's happening? [Andy begins to cry with happiness]
jokes.setup: Ben offers Andy a job at the foundation. Andy is surprised and deeply moved.
jokes.punchline: Andy's reaction to being recognized and offered a job is 'Uh-oh. What's happening?' — the emotional overwhelm expressed as mild confusion — before presumably crying.
jokes.explanation: A heartwarming Andy moment with great comedic economy. 'Uh-oh. What's happening?' as a response to being moved to happy tears is perfectly Andy — he's experiencing the emotion but doesn't quite know what to call it. Maximum character integration and economy. The joke is warm without being saccharine. Very quotable as an expression of being unexpectedly emotionally overwhelmed.

tmdb_overview: Leslie's speech she prepared for a special event is stolen. Ben begins his new job at the Sweetums Charity Foundation. Ann summons the courage to ask an important question.
insight: White House setting elevates character comedy; 65 jokes in 25 minutes sustains momentum without sacrificing craft.
